blocks.text: So much for the words. As for the sense, we have already explained the first hemistich fully and shown in what sense the wing of ostriches is said to exult, or to be glad. But concerning the second hemistich, truly the wing of the stork, and plumage, or truly a wing as of a stork, and plumage, two questions can be asked. 1. What is the point of that affirmation, TRULY a wing, and plumage? 2. Why is it called the wing and plumage of a stork, or as of a stork? To the first I answer that the ostrich is a bird that is not a bird, which in many respects approaches the nature of a quadruped. This was long ago observed by the Philosopher in book 4 of On the Parts, near the end. His words are: It has some features proper to a bird and some proper to a quadruped. That it is not a quadruped is suggested by its having feathers; that it is not a bird, by its not flying aloft and having feathers not suited to flight but hair-like. Moreover, like a quadruped it has upper eyelashes, and it is bare on the head and on the upper part of the neck, so that its eyelashes are rather hairy. But, like a bird, its lower parts are covered with plumage. And it is two-footed like a bird, but cloven-hoofed like a quadruped. For it does not have toes but a divided hoof; the cause of this is its size, which is not that of a bird but of a quadruped. Hence Diodorus, on Arabia, in book 2: Φέρει δὲ καὶ ζῶα διφυῆ, καὶ μεμιγμένα ταῖς ἰδέαις, ὧν αἱ μὲν ὀνομαζόμεναι στρουθοκάμηλοι περιειλήφασι τοῖς τύποις μίγματα χηνῶν, καὶ καμήλων· [Pherei de kai zōa diphyē, kai memigmena tais ideais, hōn hai men onomazomenai strouthokamēloi perieilēphasi tois typois migmata chēnōn, kai kamēlōn] It also produces animals of a double nature and of two forms, among which those called ostriches have an appearance mixed of geese and camels. For χηνῶν [chēnōn] read πτηνῶν [ptēnōn], because, having proved this part by part, he concludes that the ostrich χερσαῖον ἅμα φαίνεσθαι, καὶ πτηνὸν [chersaion hama phainesthai, kai ptēnon], seems at once a land animal and a winged one. Hence Herodotus calls them στρουθὸς καταγαίους [strouthous katagaious], that is, ground sparrows. And Pliny writes that they are almost of the genus of beasts. And Tertullian: A beast of some kind rather than a bird. And Alkazuinius: حيوان مركب من خلقة الطير والجمل [ḥayawān murakkab min khilqat al-ṭayr wa-l-jamal] It is an animal composed of the nature of a bird and of a camel. Hence there is a proverb of the Arabs in Damir, about one [col. 249] who is inconsistent and does not distinguish good from bad: النعامة لا طير ولا جمل [al-naʿāma lā ṭayr wa-lā jamal] The ostrich is neither bird nor camel. Accordingly, in Fable 28 of Gabrias [II, 853], when the wild beasts and the birds were disputing with each other, Λίβυσσα στρουθὸς [Libyssa strouthos], the Libyan ostrich, deceived both sides, since it seemed
Εἶναι μὲν ὄρνις, ἐκ μέρους δὲ θηρίον, Πτηνοῖς κάραν δεικνύσα, τοῖς θερσὶ πόδας, [Einai men ornis, ek merous de thērion, Ptēnois karan deiknysa, tois thersi podas,]

To be a bird indeed, but in part a wild beast, showing its head to the birds and its feet to the beasts. Since, then, this animal has so much of the quadruped, it is described here by the sacred writer together with the wild quadrupeds. And because it might seem a παράδοξος [paradoxos] thing that such an animal should have feathers and plumage like true birds, it is therefore set forth with this affirmation: Truly a wing, etc., and plumage; supply they have. Nor is it obscure why it is said to have not only feathers but the feathers of a stork. In the colour of its feathers the ostrich plainly resembles the stork. Marmol, in the place cited above: En las alas y en la cola tiene grandes plumas negras y blancas, come las de la cigueña. In its wings and tail it has large feathers, black and white, like the feathers of the stork. Hence Scaliger ^{i)}, criticizing Cardano for attributing to the ostrich blue, white, black, red and green feathers, with which soldiers' helmets are adorned, says: The colours provoke laughter which you have transferred from the dyers' workshops into the storehouses of nature. For who would not laugh at you, peddling the claim that these colours which they fix on helmets are native to ostriches? For all are marked with dusky and white, as many African merchants told me. That I might understand it better, they compared it to the colour of the stork. This verse, thus explained, will shed light on those that follow ^{(3)}.
